note: Readings worth keeping. One entry per piece. Points are short quotes or paraphrases; a quote is marked. Tags name the site page the point bears on.

entries.title: A decade of war, and the rules that are supposed to hold
entries.source: The New York Times Magazine, The Interview
entries.who: Mirjana Spoljaric, president of the International Committee of the Red Cross since 2022. She goes to both sides of wars: Gaza, Ukraine, Myanmar, Iran, Iraq, Sudan, Mali.
entries.why: She counts the wars for a living, and her account of conflicts joining into systems is the thing the map is trying to draw.

points.text: The ICRC classifies 130 armed conflicts, international and not. That is twice as many as fifteen years ago and the most since the Second World War.
We live in a decade of war.
Today's conflicts are not limited to a given situation. They are turning into systems.

What a system looks like: countries aligning across continents, shifts in military cooperation and in economic goals, and armed groups that share ideas, trade arms, and move cheap weapons and technology across thousands of kilometres. If Yemen escalates it will not stay in Yemen.
You already have two very important sea straits affected.

War is no longer a last resort. Parties keep ready to go back to fighting at any point in a negotiation, so talks take longer and need more compromise. The Iran talks are harder than the 2013 to 2015 nuclear talks for that reason.
The economic side: no growth, development gains lost fast, and countries without the fiscal room to absorb the cost of continued war. Iraq spent ten years recovering and is losing it.
War used to be a means to a political end. Now it looks like the end itself, because some leaders can only keep ruling while the war goes on.
In history, there has never been total victory; there has only been death and destruction, over and above what was necessary.
On whether a third world war has begun: history will judge. The ICRC did not know it was in the Second World War while it was happening.
If you don't negotiate over 10 years, you lose the practice.
An ANC official told her their adversaries had never negotiated anything and had to be trained before they could sit at the table.
Language at the UN has been eroding for twenty-five years. A leader who says there are no rules and no red lines is heard by everyone who carries a weapon.
Two standards are being applied: for some people bare survival in rubble counts as enough, for others only a return to normal does. If you allow double standards, it can happen to you.

The ICRC had no access to the hostages in Gaza. Israel ended the ICRC's decades of access to its detainees after 7 October 2023. Under the Geneva Conventions access is an obligation, and torture is never allowed.
On neutrality: you tweak it once, you become political, and that's it. Without 160 years of it the hostage returns and the prisoner exchanges in Ukraine would not have been trusted to the ICRC.
The Geneva Conventions, rewritten today, would come back with the same principles. Nobody in any culture will tell you it is correct to torture a child.
What to do: retreat from the overfocus on weapons and defence technology, and rebuild a positive case for peace. Her children still imagine peace as their future.

entries.title: Nearly a billion barrels drawn from the world's oil stocks
entries.source: Reuters, with the fuller speech in The National
entries.who: Sultan Al Jaber, chief executive of ADNOC, the Abu Dhabi state oil company, opening the ADIPEC conference in Abu Dhabi on 2 November 2026. He is a seller of oil and was asking for storage and refineries to be built nearer the buyers, so the figure is his estimate and no outside tally backs it yet.
entries.why: It is the first running total of what the Hormuz disruption has cost the world in stored oil. The war began on 28 February, 247 days before he spoke, so a billion barrels is about 4 million barrels a day of shortfall after rerouting, reserve releases and lost demand. That sits inside the gap between what U.S. officials claim is moving through the strait and what the trackers see. The U.S. reserve alone has given up about 130 million barrels since the shock, roughly an eighth of his total.

points.text: Nearly one billion barrels have been drawn from global oil inventories since shipping through the Strait of Hormuz was disrupted. He gave no start date and no split between commercial stocks and strategic reserves.
Simply put, the world has eroded its supply buffers.
Diesel stocks in some markets are at their lowest seasonal level in 35 years, and some markets face a gap of 600 billion cubic feet in gas supplies.
Shipping and logistics were under 5 percent of the cost of a barrel before the disruption. They are now over 30 percent.
For years, our industry optimised for just in time. This year we got the bill for just in case.
His ask: more strategic storage, larger stockpiles of refined products, and flexible refining near the markets that use the oil. Supply only counts when it arrives.

entries.title: Neither war nor peace, and the order to end it
entries.source: Press TV, with Anadolu's rendering of the same remarks
entries.who: Masoud Pezeshkian, president of Iran, speaking in Tehran on 9 November 2026 at the 72nd anniversary of the state dairy company. He is a party to the war, and the Supreme Leader's order is known only through his account of it. Press TV is Iranian state television; Anadolu is Turkey's state news agency and carries a second English rendering of the same lines.
entries.why: Iran's name for the state this site is built around is 'neither war nor peace'. The site calls it the perpetual war sweet spot and reads it off the oil price: BNO between 49 and 55. Here is the president of the country on the other side of the war saying the same thing, and saying the order has come down to end it. He would agree we are living in perpetual war. The argument is only about the price band: when he spoke, BNO's last close was 62.22, which the heuristic calls war, not the sweet spot.

points.text: The Leader has instructed us to put an end to the current state of neither war nor peace.
We can engage in dialogue with dignity and bring this matter to a dignified conclusion.
Logic dictates that if we can secure our rights through dialogue, we should avoid becoming embroiled in war.
However, we will never surrender in the face of force, intimidation, or bullying.

Not the first time. He said Iran 'must get out of the neither war nor peace policy' on 10 June, at a memorial for the late Supreme Leader, who he said had repeatedly asked for it to be resolved. He said it again at a press conference on 8 August ('war cannot continue forever'), to the cabinet on 28 October, and at a fuel-rationing meeting on 7 November. The 9 November line is the first to say the new Leader has ordered it.
